chunks.title: The tear film: 3 layers
chunks.tldr: Tears = oil on top (meibomian), water in the middle (lacrimal), mucus at the bottom (goblet cells).
points: Lipid layer (meibomian glands): stops evaporation, helps tears spread. Missing → evaporative dry eye.
Aqueous layer (main lacrimal gland ~95%, plus accessory glands of Krause and Wolfring): oxygen, antibacterial (IgA, lysozyme, lactoferrin), washes debris, smooths the optics.
Reflex tearing goes through CN V. Drops during sleep and with anaesthetic drops. Can rise 500% with injury.
Mucous layer (goblet cells): makes the cornea wettable (hydrophobic → hydrophilic).
Goblet cells are lost in: OCP, vitamin A deficiency, chemical burns, drug toxicity.
Spreading tears needs: a normal blink, lids touching the eye, healthy epithelium.
Hormones: androgens control lipid production.
chunks.hook: Like a sandwich: oil on top, water in the middle, mucus 'butter' stuck to the cornea.

chunks.title: Types of dry eye (DEWS)
chunks.tldr: Two big types: aqueous-deficient (not enough tears) and evaporative (tears dry up too fast). Most people have both.
points: Core problem: unstable tears → high osmolarity → inflammation (in 80%) → surface damage → repeat.
Aqueous-deficient: Sjögren (primary/secondary) or non-Sjögren.
Non-Sjögren: age, gland infiltration (sarcoid, lymphoma, GVHD, AIDS), blocked ducts (trachoma, OCP, SJS, chemical), poor reflex (contact lenses, diabetes, LASIK, neurotrophic, CN VII palsy, drugs).
Evaporative, intrinsic: MGD/rosacea, wide lid gap (proptosis, retraction), low blink rate (screens, Parkinson), drugs (antihistamines, beta-blockers, diuretics).
Evaporative, extrinsic: vitamin A deficiency, preservatives, contact lenses, allergy.
Words: KCS = any dry eye. Xerophthalmia = vitamin A deficiency. Xerosis = extreme dryness + keratinisation from scarring.

chunks.title: Sjögren syndrome
chunks.tldr: Autoimmune attack on tear and salivary glands: dry eyes + dry mouth + big parotids. Check anti-SSA/SSB (Ro/La).
points: Lymphocytes destroy the exocrine glands.
Primary = on its own (mostly women). Secondary = with RA or SLE.
ACR criteria: anti-SSA/SSB (or RF + ANA), ocular surface staining score, labial salivary gland biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis.
Treat: dry-eye measures, oral pilocarpine/cevimeline (for mouth and eyes), immunosuppression, rituximab.
(Sjögren patients have a higher risk of lymphoma.)

chunks.title: Dry eye symptoms & signs
chunks.tldr: Gritty, burning, worse as the day goes on and with wind, air-con, screens. Signs: thin meniscus, debris, PEEs, filaments.
points: Symptoms: dry, gritty, burning, stringy discharge, blur that clears with blinking.
Worse with: air-conditioning, wind, heating, reading, screens (fewer blinks).
Often also has posterior blepharitis / MGD.
Tear film: mucus debris, thin meniscus (<0.25 mm; normal 0.2–0.4).
Conjunctiva: red, stains with rose Bengal/lissamine, conjunctivochalasis.
Cornea: punctate erosions, filaments (strands stuck at one end), mucous plaques.
Severe: melt, perforation, bacterial keratitis.
chunks.hook: Dry eye feels like sand that gets worse by evening.

chunks.title: Dry eye tests
chunks.tldr: Key numbers: TBUT <10 s. Schirmer <10 mm (no anaesthetic) or <6 mm (with anaesthetic) in 5 min. Osmolarity ≥308.
points: Order: TBUT → staining → Schirmer (the Schirmer strip itself causes staining).
TBUT: fluorescein, blink, time to the first dry spot. <10 s is suspicious. Same spot every time → local surface problem (e.g. EBMD).
Schirmer: strip at the junction of the middle and outer third of the lower lid, eyes closed, 5 min. Without anaesthetic (Schirmer 1) <10 mm abnormal. With anaesthetic <6 mm abnormal.
Fluorescein = damaged epithelium. Rose Bengal = dead cells/no mucin (stings!). Lissamine green = like rose Bengal but gentler.
Staining pattern: interpalpebral → aqueous deficiency. Superior → SLK. Inferior → blepharitis or exposure.
Osmolarity: ≥308 mOsm/L dry. ≥316 → moderate–severe.
Others: MMP-9 (raised), lactoferrin (low), phenol red thread (<6 mm in 15 s), impression cytology (goblet cells).
Symptoms often don't match the tests. Tests get more reliable in severe cases.
chunks.hook: Remember 10-10-6: TBUT 10 s, Schirmer 10 mm without anaesthetic, 6 mm with.

cards.q: Abnormal Schirmer value with topical anaesthesia?

cards.a: The Schirmer strip irritates the surface and causes staining.

chunks.title: Dry eye treatment ladder (levels 1–4)
chunks.tldr: Step up: 1 lifestyle + tears + lid care → 2 preservative-free, anti-inflammatory, plugs → 3 serum drops, contact lenses, permanent occlusion → 4 systemic drugs, surgery.
points: Level 1: education, blink breaks, screen below eye level, humidity, stop bad drugs and preserved drops, tear substitutes, warm compress + lid hygiene, tape lids for night lagophthalmos. Warn that LASIK can worsen it.

Level 2: preservative-free tears, topical steroid short course, ciclosporin, omega-3, doxycycline, punctal plugs, secretagogues (pilocarpine, cevimeline, diquafosol, rebamipide), moisture-chamber glasses.
Level 3: autologous serum (or cord serum, finger-prick blood), therapeutic contact lenses, permanent punctal occlusion.
Level 4: systemic anti-inflammatories, tarsorrhaphy, salivary gland transplant, mucous/amniotic membrane grafts.
chunks.hook: Climb the ladder: Habits → Tears → Calm the inflammation → Plug → Serum → Surgery.

cards.q: Topical drug that reduces T-cell inflammation and increases goblet cells?
Name a level 3 dry eye treatment.
cards.a: Autologous serum drops (or contact lenses, permanent punctal occlusion).

chunks.title: Tear substitutes, plugs & more
chunks.tldr: Use preservative-free drops if dosing more than 4× a day. Try a temporary plug first, then make it permanent if there's no watering.
points: Drops: cellulose (mild), carbomer gels (last longer, blur a bit), PVA, hyaluronate. No single one is best.
Ointment (paraffin) at night only (blurs).
Acetylcysteine 5% dissolves filaments and mucous plaques (stings, smells).
Preservatives (BAK) are toxic, especially after plugging. Newer ones (Polyquad, Purite) are gentler.
Punctal occlusion: collagen (temporary, dissolves) → if no watering after 1–2 weeks → silicone or cautery (permanent). Lower puncta first. Never all 4 at once.
Plug problems: falling out, granuloma, migrating into the canaliculus.
Contact lenses: reservoir effect, but higher keratitis risk. Scleral lenses for severe cases.
Others: lower room temperature, goggles, botox for blepharospasm, oral pilocarpine (Sjögren).
chunks.hook: Test the plug before you seal the drain.

cards.q: Why insert temporary plugs before permanent occlusion?
cards.a: To make sure epiphora won't follow.
